title: The Detective and the Crumbs of Everything

topics.value_lesson: Unfinished pieces are not failures; sometimes they are the best records of the past.

spine: A young detective follows the trail of the solar system's leftovers to discover why the planets left so many pieces behind.

comet_name.role: The name Marisol gives the comet she spots

detective_badge_word.role: The silly word Marisol stamps on her detective notebook cover

segments.text:
It was a cold, clear night, and Detective Marisol Vega was on a stakeout.

"The backyard is quiet," whispered a tiny voice from her jacket pocket. "TOO quiet. The galaxy holds its breath!"

That was Zorp. Zorp was a small plush alien, and he narrated everything like a space epic, even breakfast.

Marisol's brother Theo stood beside her, breathing on his hands to warm them. Above them the sky was black and deep and sprinkled with stars, and somewhere up there was a comet nobody in their family had spotted yet. Marisol intended to be the first.

"Binoculars up," she said.

"Binoculars UP!" squeaked Zorp. "The brave detective raises her mighty—"

"Zorp."

"Sorry. Quiet. Too quiet. Got it."

Marisol swept the binoculars slowly across the sky. Roof. Chimney. Stars. Stars. And then—

"There!" She grabbed Theo's sleeve. "There it is! I found it!"

The comet hung in the dark like a fuzzy crumb on a bakery counter, with a long glowing tail streaming off to one side.

Marisol lowered the binoculars. Then she raised them again. Then she lowered them again.

"Theo," she said slowly. "Comet tails point away from the sun. That's the rule. The sun is down there, behind the hills. So the tail should point up."

"And?"

"The tail points sideways."

Theo squinted. "Maybe it's... a relaxed comet?"

"Comets don't relax."

From her pocket came a gasp. "A MYSTERY! In the cold depths of space, a clue appears—"

Marisol pulled out her detective notebook and clicked her pen. "Case number one," she said. "The comet with the sideways tail. I'm calling it {comet_name}."

She wrote the name at the top of a fresh page, then stamped the cover with her favorite word: {detective_badge_word}.

"The Case of the Cosmic Crumbs," she said, "is officially open."

The next morning, Marisol and Theo pedaled to the space museum, Zorp bouncing in her pocket like a very dramatic popcorn kernel.

"The heroes approach the Temple of Ancient Stones!" he squeaked.

Inside, the guide smiled at Marisol's notebook. "You want the meteorite case. End of the hall."

And there it was. A dark little rock under glass, no bigger than a bar of soap, with a bumpy crust like the edge of burnt toast.

"That," said the guide, "is a piece of an asteroid. It fell out of the sky and landed in a farmer's field. And here's the wild part — it's older than any rock on Earth. Older than the mountains. Older than the oceans."

Marisol pressed both hands to the glass. "Older than everything?"

"Older than everything here."

"A MESSAGE IN A BOTTLE!" Zorp declared, popping up. "Flung across the endless void from the dawn of TIME ITSELF!"

"Zorp, it's a rock."

"It's a rock that REMEMBERS."

Marisol flipped her notebook open to the sketch of {comet_name} and held it beside the case. Crumb on a bakery counter. Crumb under glass. Both leftovers. Both from the very beginning, when the planets were still forming.

"Theo," she whispered. "This rock was there. At the formation of the whole solar system. It's a clue that fell out of the sky on purpose."

"Rocks don't do things on purpose."

"Then it's a clue that fell out of the sky by accident, and I don't care, because look at it."

Theo leaned in close. "So if the comet's a crumb and this is a crumb..."

"Then somebody," Marisol said, "left crumbs all over the solar system. And I want to know why."

"DUN DUN DUN," said Zorp.

That evening, Marisol and Theo climbed the hill to the observatory, where Dr. Okafor had the big telescope aimed at a faint, slow-moving dot.

"An asteroid," she said, stepping aside so Marisol could look. "There it goes. One of millions."

"MILLIONS!" squeaked Zorp. "A mighty swarm, packed shoulder to shoulder in the cold dark—"

"Actually," said Dr. Okafor, "that's the funny part." She pulled out a chart of the solar system and tapped the ring between Mars and Jupiter. "This is the asteroid belt. In pictures it looks like a crowded rock field. Ships dodging, rocks bonking into each other. But that's not true. The belt is almost entirely empty space."

Marisol looked up. "Empty?"

"If you stood on one asteroid, you probably couldn't even see the next one. They're spread out over millions and millions of kilometers. All the asteroids together weigh less than the Moon."

There was a small thump. Zorp had fainted backward into Marisol's pocket.

"The pictures LIE," he moaned. "The epic space chase through the deadly rock field... a fantasy!"

"But wait." Marisol pulled out her notebook, flipping to the sketch of {comet_name}. "If they're leftovers from the formation of the solar system — crumbs from when the planets got baked — why are they spread out? Crumbs don't spread themselves. Somebody sweeps them."

Dr. Okafor raised one eyebrow. "Somebody... or something. Something big enough to stir a whole belt."

Theo looked at the chart. Then at the telescope. Then at Marisol. "Something big," he repeated. "Like, planet big?"

"Jupiter big," said Dr. Okafor.

Marisol clicked her pen and wrote one word on the page, in capital letters: SUSPECT.

"The Case of the Cosmic Crumbs," she said, "just got a lot bigger."

"DUN DUN DUN," said a muffled voice from her pocket.

Back inside, Marisol spread her notebook open on the kitchen table and clicked her pen twice, which was her thinking sound. "Okay," she said. "Tell me everything. What did you find out there?"

Theo talked. Zorp added trumpets. Marisol wrote it all down, and when they were done she tapped the page. "So now we have this, plus the sideways tail. The Sun pushes a comet's tail around like wind pushing smoke. That's clue one."

"Clue one!" Zorp squeaked from her pocket. "The detective's mighty brain awakens!"

Marisol pulled out the model they'd built last week, the one with little balls for planets. She pointed at the space between Mars and Jupiter, where they'd scattered a whole handful of crumbs and pebbles. "The asteroid belt. Millions of chunks, all circling, and they never got together into a planet. You know why? Jupiter. It's so big its gravity kept stirring them, like a spoon in a pot that never stops. The pieces kept bumping and flying apart. They never got to build."

Theo frowned. "So the planets formed all neat and tidy, but—"

"But why are so many pieces still wandering?" Marisol finished. She wrote the question in big letters. Then she stared at it. Then she gasped so hard Zorp nearly fell out of her pocket.

"Leftovers," she whispered. "Theo. The asteroids, the comets — they're leftovers. From the formation of the whole solar system. When everything formed, most of the dust and rock baked into planets. But these bits never got used. They're the crumbs that never became cake."

"Crumbs," Theo breathed.

"And because they never got baked, they never changed. They still remember the beginning. Every comet, every asteroid — it's a piece of day one, still floating around."

Zorp made a strange sound. Marisol looked down. The little alien was weeping, tiny plush tears on his tiny plush cheeks. "The crumbs," he whispered, "are the TREASURE MAP. The greatest case in the galaxy, solved by—"

"Not solved yet," said Marisol, standing up. Because a real detective with an answer this big had to do something about it. But what?

Family night at the museum was loud. Kids everywhere, sticky fingers, a dinosaur skeleton towering over the lobby. Marisol stood beside the meteorite case, notebook in hand, Zorp riding shotgun in her pocket.

"Citizens of Earth!" Zorp squeaked. "The detective prepares to reveal the greatest secret in the—"

"Zorp."

"Right. Quiet."

Dr. Okafor tapped the microphone. "Everyone, this is Marisol. She has something to tell you about that little dark rock."

Marisol stepped up. The rock sat behind the glass, small and gray and ordinary. Nobody ever looked at it twice.

"This rock is a crumb," she said. "From the bakery of the beginning. When the solar system formed, most of the dust and rock baked into planets. But some pieces never got used. They never changed. They still remember day one."

She pointed at the asteroid belt poster. "The asteroid belt is full of crumbs. Comets too. They're leftovers, and they're the oldest things you can touch."

A little kid in the front row gasped. "That rock remembers the beginning?"

"That rock IS the beginning," said Marisol.

Dr. Okafor smiled and peeled a sticker off a sheet. It said JUNIOR DETECTIVE in silver letters. She pressed it onto Marisol's notebook, right next to the name {comet_name}.

"Case closed," said Dr. Okafor.

"Case CLOSED!" Zorp shouted. "The galaxy rejoices!"

On the way out, Marisol stopped at the gift table. She picked up a postcard of Ceres, the quiet round world hiding among the crumbs, and tucked it into her notebook.

"You coming?" Theo asked.

"Yeah," said Marisol, patting her pocket. "We're coming."

The backyard was cold again, but Marisol didn't mind. The comet was leaving, and she had to see it off.

"There," said Dr. Okafor, pointing through the telescope. "Still got that sideways tail."

Marisol looked. The comet hung in the dark, fuzzy and glowing, its tail streaming off at that strange angle. The Sun's invisible fan, pushing the tail around like wind pushing smoke.

"It's a dirty snowball from the beginning," Marisol said. "A crumb that never got baked. And it's been carrying that memory for billions of years."

"Billions," Theo breathed.

Zorp sniffled from her pocket. "The brave crumb sails into the void, alone but unforgotten—"

"Zorp."

"Sorry."

Marisol pulled out her notebook and clicked her pen. She wrote the final entry: "Comet {comet_name}. Dirty snowball. Tail blown sideways by the Sun's fan. Leftover from the formation of everything. Case closed."

She underlined the name twice.

"You're really naming it {comet_name}?" Theo asked.

"I already did," said Marisol. "It's official. It's in the notebook."

Dr. Okafor handed her something small and heavy. A meteorite replica from the observatory gift table, dark and pocked and cool to the touch.

"A crumb that remembers," said Dr. Okafor.

Marisol held it up to the sky. The comet was already fading, already sailing away into the deep black. It would be gone for years.

"Goodbye, {comet_name}," she whispered.

She tucked the meteorite into her pocket, next to Zorp, and patted it once.

"Come on," she said. "Let's go inside. I'm keeping this on my windowsill."
